title: Paul's Journey to Rome
overview: Acts 28 concludes the Book of Acts by detailing Paul's shipwreck on the island of Melita, his ministry there, and his eventual arrival in Rome. The chapter highlights God's providential protection over Paul, the miraculous healings he performs, and his bold witness to both Jews and Gentiles. It underscores the expansion of the gospel to the Gentile world, fulfilling Jesus' command to be witnesses unto the ends of the earth. Paul's two-year house arrest in Rome serves as a powerful testimony of faithfulness and perseverance, as he preaches the kingdom of God with confidence despite his chains. This chapter serves as a fitting climax to the missionary journeys recorded in Acts, emphasizing God's sovereignty and the unstoppable advance of the gospel.
structure:
**Verses 1-10: Shipwreck and Ministry on Melita.** After surviving a shipwreck, Paul and the others find refuge on Melita where Paul’s miraculous healing of Publius’ father and others establishes goodwill and divine favor.

**Verses 11-16: Journey to Rome.** Paul and companions continue their journey by ship and land, receiving warm welcomes from fellow believers, which encourages Paul as he approaches the center of the Roman Empire.

**Verses 17-29: Paul’s Ministry to the Jewish Leaders in Rome.** Paul calls the Jewish leaders, explains his imprisonment and appeal to Caesar, and boldly proclaims the gospel, warning of Israel’s spiritual blindness and declaring salvation now extended to the Gentiles.

**Verses 30-31: Paul’s Two-Year Ministry in Rome.** Despite being a prisoner, Paul freely preaches and teaches about Jesus Christ with full confidence, marking the gospel’s firm establishment in Rome and the wider Gentile world.

keyVerses.text: Howbeit they looked when he should have swollen, or fallen down dead suddenly: but after they had looked a great while , and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds, and said that he was a god.
keyVerses.significance: This verse demonstrates God's protection over Paul, affirming his divine mission. The islanders’ change of mind from suspicion to reverence highlights the power of God working through Paul, setting the stage for his ministry on Melita.

keyVerses.text: Be it known therefore unto you, that the salvation of God is sent unto the Gentiles, and that they will hear it.
keyVerses.significance: This pivotal declaration marks the gospel’s expansion beyond Israel to the Gentiles, fulfilling God’s promise and Jesus’ commission. It underscores the inclusive nature of salvation and the shift in the early church’s mission.

keyVerses.text: And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him,
keyVerses.significance: Paul’s two-year residence in Rome, despite imprisonment, illustrates the unstoppable spread of the gospel. It shows that physical chains could not hinder Paul’s ministry or the proclamation of Christ.

keyVerses.text: Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him.
keyVerses.significance: This verse emphasizes Paul’s boldness and freedom in preaching the gospel even while under house arrest. It highlights the confidence believers can have in God’s power to advance His kingdom despite opposition.

characters.name: Paul
characters.description: The apostle and central figure of this chapter, Paul survives a shipwreck, performs miracles, and boldly preaches the gospel in Rome. His faithfulness and perseverance exemplify Christian witness under trial.

characters.name: Publius
characters.description: The chief man of Melita who hospitably receives Paul and his companions. His father’s healing by Paul leads to many others being healed, showing the impact of divine power and hospitality.

characters.name: Jewish Leaders in Rome
characters.description: They meet with Paul to hear his defense and teaching. Their mixed response reflects the ongoing tension and division regarding the acceptance of Jesus as Messiah.

characters.name: Islanders of Melita
characters.description: Initially suspicious of Paul after the viper bite, they later honor him as a god when he suffers no harm. Their response illustrates human reactions to divine intervention and the power of God’s protection.

themes.description: God’s sovereign care is evident in Paul’s survival of the shipwreck and protection from the viper’s venom. This theme reassures believers of God’s control over circumstances and His care for His servants.

themes.theme: The Expansion of the Gospel to the Gentiles
themes.description: Paul’s ministry on Melita and in Rome, along with his declaration that salvation is sent to the Gentiles, highlights the fulfillment of God’s promise to bless all nations through Christ.
Paul’s continued preaching despite imprisonment exemplifies steadfastness in trials. This encourages believers to remain faithful and confident in God’s mission regardless of hardships.

Paul’s message to the Jewish leaders about their hardened hearts reflects the biblical theme of judgment upon those who reject God’s revelation, while also pointing to the hope of salvation for those who believe.

historicalContext: Acts 28 is set around AD 60-62 during Paul’s journey to Rome, the heart of the Roman Empire. The island of Melita (modern Malta) was a known stopover in the Mediterranean, inhabited by 'barbarous' people, a term used by Romans to describe non-Greek-speaking natives. Hospitality was a valued custom, as seen in Publius’ reception of Paul. Rome was the political and cultural center of the empire, where Paul’s appeal to Caesar brought him under house arrest but also provided a platform for gospel proclamation. The Jewish community in Rome was significant, and tensions between Jewish and Gentile believers were ongoing, reflected in Paul’s interactions with Jewish leaders.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes God’s sovereign providence in Paul’s journey and ministry, viewing the shipwreck and healing miracles as demonstrations of God’s covenant faithfulness and power to advance His kingdom despite opposition.

Dispensationalists highlight the distinct roles of Israel and the Church, interpreting Paul’s message to the Jews in Rome as a postponement of Israel’s national restoration and the opening of the gospel to the Gentiles as a new dispensation.

Early church fathers saw Paul’s sufferings and bold preaching as a model of apostolic endurance and the fulfillment of Christ’s promise that the gospel would reach the ends of the earth, emphasizing the unity of God’s plan for Jew and Gentile.

crossReferences.connection: Paul’s bold preaching of the gospel in Rome echoes his declaration that the gospel is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes.
Paul’s quotation of Isaiah about hearing but not understanding highlights Israel’s spiritual blindness, a key theme in Acts 28.
The expansion of the gospel to the Gentiles in Acts 28 fulfills Jesus’ Great Commission to make disciples of all nations.
Paul’s confidence in preaching despite imprisonment reflects his testimony of God’s presence and deliverance in trials.
The kindness of the Melita islanders parallels the Good Samaritan’s compassion, illustrating Christian hospitality and care.

application: Trust God’s providence in difficult circumstances, knowing He controls all events for His glory.
Be faithful in witnessing for Christ even when facing opposition or imprisonment.
Extend hospitality and kindness to others as a reflection of God’s love.
Recognize the importance of preaching the gospel to all people, Jew and Gentile alike.
Pray for spiritual understanding and openness among those who resist the gospel.
Remain confident in God’s promises and power to sustain His servants.
conclusion: Acts 28 powerfully concludes the Book of Acts by showcasing God’s sovereign hand in Paul’s journey and ministry. The chapter reveals the unstoppable advance of the gospel to the Gentile world, the faithfulness required in suffering, and the spiritual realities of acceptance and rejection of Christ. Paul’s example encourages believers to trust God’s providence, boldly proclaim the kingdom of God, and extend grace to all people. His two-year ministry in Rome under house arrest affirms that no earthly chains can hinder the spread of God’s salvation, making this chapter a timeless encouragement for the church’s mission today.
timeline: c. AD 60-62 - Paul’s journey to Rome, shipwreck on Melita, and two-year house arrest in Rome

outline.heading: Shipwreck and Divine Protection on Melita
outline.description: Paul and companions survive a shipwreck and receive kindness from the islanders. Paul’s miraculous healing of Publius’ father and others confirms God’s power and favor.

outline.heading: Journey and Arrival in Rome
outline.description: Paul continues his journey to Rome, receiving encouragement from fellow believers along the way, culminating in his arrival and house arrest.

outline.heading: Paul’s Defense and Gospel Proclamation to Jewish Leaders
outline.description: Paul explains his imprisonment and appeals to Caesar, boldly preaching the kingdom of God and declaring salvation for the Gentiles, while addressing Israel’s spiritual blindness.

outline.heading: Paul’s Ministry in Rome under House Arrest
outline.description: Despite imprisonment, Paul preaches and teaches with confidence, demonstrating that the gospel cannot be hindered by physical chains.
